content: Cholestasis is a medical condition characterized by the inability of bile to flow from the liver to the duodenum. Bile formation is a critical secretory function of the liver. This process begins in bile canaliculi, which are small channels formed between adjacent surfaces of liver cells, or hepatocytes, resembling the terminal branches of a tree. These canaliculi merge to form progressively larger structures, sometimes referred to as the Canals of Hering. These structures eventually connect to form small bile ductules lined with epithelial cells. The ductules then join to form bile ducts, which ultimately converge into either the right main hepatic duct, draining the right lobe of the liver, or the left main hepatic duct, draining the left lobe. These two ducts unite to form the common hepatic duct, which subsequently joins the cystic duct from the gallbladder to create the common bile duct. The common bile duct then empties into the duodenum at the ampulla of Vater. Cholestasis can be classified into two main types. The obstructive type occurs when there is a mechanical blockage in the bile duct system, such as from gallstones or malignancies. The metabolic type arises from disturbances in bile formation, which may result from genetic defects or as an adverse effect of certain medications. On a microscopic level, hepatocytes in cholestasis exhibit a brownish-green stippled appearance within their cytoplasm, representing bile that is trapped and unable to exit the cell. Canalicular bile plugs may also be observed between individual hepatocytes or within bile ducts, indicating bile that has been excreted from the hepatocytes but cannot progress further due to obstruction. In cases where these plugs occur within the bile ducts, the accumulation of bile can generate sufficient pressure to cause ductal rupture. This leads to the spillage of bile into the surrounding tissue, resulting in hepatic necrosis. These necrotic areas, known as bile lakes, are typically associated with extra-hepatic obstruction. Laboratory findings in cholestasis often reveal elevated levels of bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase in blood tests, which are indicative of impaired bile flow and liver dysfunction.
